Here’s Tier 1 and Tier 2 in plain terms, tied to **your app today** and **your benchmark numbers**.

---

## The problem today

Every time you search, open All Contacts, or open Recent, the app does roughly this:

1. **Load every `Node` from SwiftData** (`FetchDescriptor<Node>()` — all ~10,026 after your stress import)
2. **Filter, walk connections, and sort in memory** in Swift

Your baseline on ~10k nodes:

- **Search:** ~400 ms per query (same work every time, even repeat queries like `"1021"`)
- **Import:** ~6.4 s (separate problem — bulk insert)
- **All Contacts / Recent:** noticeable delay on open (same “fetch all nodes” pattern, then filter to masters and sort)

Debouncing (waiting 0.3 s after you stop typing) only reduces *how often* this runs. It does **not** make each run cheaper.

Tier 1 and Tier 2 attack **how expensive each run is**, without changing what search *means* (same rules: word-start matching, connections, AND for multiple keywords).

---

## What both tiers have in common

| | Tier 1 | Tier 2 |
|--|--------|--------|
| **SwiftData / CloudKit schema** | No change | No change |
| **Search rules** | Identical results | Identical results (must be verified) |
| **Ship target** | Production + Test | Production + Test |
| **Risk** | Low | Low–moderate (index must stay in sync) |

---

## Tier 1 — “Stop redoing the same expensive work”

Tier 1 is **engineering around** the current design. Same algorithm, smarter execution.

### 1. Cache the node fetch (session cache)

**Today:** Every search calls `fetch(all nodes)` — even your 4th search for `"1021"` reloads all 10,026 nodes from SQLite.

**Tier 1:** Keep the fetched `[Node]` array in memory for a **session** (or until the graph changes). Reuse it for the next search in that session.

- **First search after open or after an edit:** still pays full fetch cost (~400 ms in your test)
- **Repeat searches, or 2nd keyword in same session:** skip the DB read; only run the in-memory graph logic

Also applies to **All Contacts / Recent** if we cache the **master list** and only rebuild when something was added/edited/deleted/imported since last view — that’s the fix for the delay you noticed after import.

### 2. Run search off the main thread

**Today:** Search runs on the **main thread** → UI can stutter or feel frozen during those ~400 ms.

**Tier 1:** Do the fetch + filter on a **background** queue/task; update results on main when done. Same work, but Home stays responsive (spinner / old results until new ones arrive).

### 3. Debounce tuning

You already debounce Home search at 0.3 s. Tier 1 may tweak that slightly, but debounce alone was never the main fix — caching and background work are.

### What Tier 1 does **not** do

- It does **not** reduce work from O(all nodes) to O(small subset) on the **first** search after a fresh fetch.
- Your ~400 ms baseline might drop some (background = smoother UI), but the **first** full scan is still “touch every node” unless Tier 2 helps.

**Analogy:** Tier 1 is like keeping the phone book on your desk instead of walking to the shelf every time you look up a name. You still read the whole book if you have to scan page by page — but you stop making the trip repeatedly, and you can read while someone else uses the desk (UI).

---

## Tier 2 — “Word index so we don’t scan everyone”

Tier 2 adds an **in-memory index** built from existing node labels. **Nothing new in the database** — RAM only, rebuilt when data changes.

### How it would work

When the graph loads or changes (add/edit/delete/import):

1. Walk all nodes once
2. Split each label into **words** (same rules as search: spaces, etc.)
3. Build a map: **`"1021"` → [node IDs that have a word starting with `"1021"`]**

When you search `"1021"`:

1. Look up `"1021"` in the index → maybe **1–50 candidate nodes**, not 10,026
2. Run **today’s existing graph logic** only on those candidates (connections, masters, AND logic, ranking)

Search **behavior stays the same**; we just don’t consider nodes that can’t possibly match.

### Index maintenance

The index must update when:

- You add a contact or attribute  
- You edit a label / primary / connection  
- You import or delete  

On change: update affected entries (or rebuild if simpler at first). If the index is wrong, search results would be wrong — that’s why Tier 2 needs careful testing against your Benchmarks screen (`"1021"`, multi-keyword, attribute-only hits, etc.).

### What Tier 2 improves most

- **Single-keyword search** at scale (your `"1021"` case) — could go from ~400 ms toward tens of ms, depending on hit count and device
- **Repeated searches** — especially combined with Tier 1 cache
- Less CPU per keystroke once the index exists

### What Tier 2 is trickier for

- **Multi-keyword AND** — still doable (intersect candidate sets per keyword, then run graph logic)
- **Connection traversal** — still needed for “attribute hit → show connected masters”; index narrows the *starting* set, not the whole graph semantics
- **Memory** — index lives in RAM; fine for 10k nodes, worth watching at much larger scale

**Analogy:** Tier 2 is the index at the back of the phone book. You jump to “1021” and only read the pages that matter, then still apply your normal rules about who’s linked to whom.

---

## How Tier 1 + Tier 2 fit together

```
Today:
  every search → fetch ALL nodes → scan ALL → results (~400 ms)

Tier 1 only:
  first search → fetch ALL → scan ALL → results
  next searches (same session) → scan ALL (reuse cached nodes) → faster, smoother UI

Tier 1 + Tier 2:
  first search → index lookup → scan FEW candidates → results (much faster)
  next searches → cached nodes + index → even faster
  All Contacts (if cached) → no refetch if graph unchanged
```

Recommended order: **Tier 1 first** (quick, low risk, helps UI and repeat operations), then **Tier 2** (bigger win on first search at 10k nodes).

---

## Against your baseline (what to expect)

| Operation | Today (~10k nodes) | After Tier 1 (rough) | After Tier 1 + Tier 2 (rough) |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
| Search `"1021"` (1st run) | ~400 ms | Similar CPU, **smoother UI** (background) | **Much lower** if index hits are small |
| Search `"1021"` (repeat) | ~400 ms each | **Faster** (no refetch) | **Faster still** (index + cache) |
| All Contacts open | Noticeable delay | **Better** if master list cached | **Better** (cache + maybe index build shared) |
| Import 10k JSON | ~6.4 s | Similar | Similar (import is insert work, not search) |

Import speed is a **separate** future item (chunked insert, progress UI) — not Tier 1 or Tier 2.

---

## What we’re explicitly **not** doing in Tier 1/2

- **28 A–Z buckets** — wrong fit for your word-start search rules  
- **FTS5 / new DB tables** — Tier 3+  
- **Directories partition** — separate product phase  
- **Changing CloudKit schema** — avoids sync/migration pain  

---

## How you’ll know it worked

Use **If I Must Test → Benchmarks** with `If-I-Must-stress-test-10000.json`:

1. Import (baseline **6.38 s** — for reference only)  
2. Search all `"1021"` four times — compare to **402–424 ms**  
3. Search masters `"1021"` — compare to **394–414 ms**  
4. Subjective: All Contacts / Recent open time after import  

After Tier 1/2, those numbers (and how the app *feels*) should improve; results for `"1021"` should still be **1 hit**.

---

**Short summary:**  
**Tier 1** = cache + background + smart list caching — same logic, less repeated work, UI doesn’t freeze.  
**Tier 2** = word index in RAM — same logic, but only run it on a small candidate set instead of all 10,026 nodes.

When you want to start implementation, Tier 1 is the natural first step in the Test app, then re-run your benchmark log before adding Tier 2.

## 1. Recents empty after import — expected

The stress JSON sets **every** `dateCreated` to **2026-01-01** (fixed at export).

**Recently Added** only shows masters created in the **Past Day / Week / Month**. In June 2026, January dates don’t qualify — so Recents is empty even though **All Contacts** has 10,000 masters.

That’s not a Tier 1 bug. If Recents populated on an earlier test, it was likely a different graph (real contacts with recent dates) or a different time window.

For stress-test browsing, use **All Contacts**, not Recents. Documented in `If-I-Must-Benchmarks/NOTES.md`.

---

## 2. All Contacts lag after favorite + back — fixed (Test app)

**Cause:** Tapping the star calls `markContentEdited`, which updates `dateLastEdited`. That invalidated the **full** 10k-node cache, and returning to All Contacts triggered a full reload.

**Fix (Test app only):**
- **Browse cache** (All Contacts) only invalidates when node/connection **counts** change — not on favorite/edit timestamps alone
- **All Contacts** skips reload when you navigate back if the browse cache is still valid

That first-tap delay is a classic cold-start cost: nothing is “wrong” with your data — several things were all happening the first time you opened the menu.

**What was causing it**

1. **Menu sheet building everything at once** — Each `NavigationLink { QuickGuideView() }` style link tells SwiftUI to prepare those destinations when the sheet appears. `QuickGuideView` is the heavy one (lots of localized strings and layout). First open = ~0.5–1 s of work; later opens reuse warmed views, so they feel instant.

2. **StoreKit on Test app launch** — Even with the paywall bypassed, `RootView` was still creating `SubscriptionManager` and doing subscription checks on every launch. That’s unnecessary for the Test build.

3. **Startup migrations on empty DB** — `ContentView` ran two migration passes on launch even when there were zero nodes. Small, but it’s work on the critical path.

**What I changed**

| Fix | Effect |
|-----|--------|
| Lazy menu via `navigationDestination(for:)` | Destinations build only when you tap a row, not when the sheet opens |
| `PaywallRootContent` split out of `RootView` | Test app (and Simulator bypass) skip `SubscriptionManager` entirely |
| Skip migrations when `nodeCount == 0` | No migration work on empty app after Delete All |

Build succeeded on the Test scheme.

**How to verify**

Same workflow: Delete All → stop Xcode → cold launch → tap menu immediately. The first open should feel much snappier. You may still see a tiny delay the very first time from DEBUG/Xcode attach and SwiftUI’s first sheet presentation — that’s normal and should be smaller than before.

- It happens on a **cold launch** with an **empty** app

Yes — for **benchmarking**, that’s the right call.

**Why**

Tier 1 and Tier 2 fix different things:

| | Tier 1 | Tier 2 |
|--|--------|--------|
| Main win | Cache the graph in memory + search off the main thread | Don’t scan all 10k nodes for every keyword |
| Your numbers | ~414 ms → ~48 ms search | Unknown until measured |

With Tier 1 still on, a Tier 2 benchmark mostly measures **Tier 1 + Tier 2**, not Tier 2 alone. You already know Tier 1’s numbers; the open question is what Tier 2 adds on top of the **original** path (`fetch all nodes` + `SearchService` on the main thread).

**What I’d do (not delete — disable)**

- Add a single Test-app flag, e.g. `performanceTier1Enabled = false`, and route search/browse through the **old** paths when it’s off.
- Leave `GraphPerformanceCache`, `SearchSnapshotEngine`, etc. in the project (or note the Tier 1 results in `If-I-Must-App-NOTES.md` and keep the code idle).

That gives you a clean Tier 2 score without losing Tier 1 work.

- Search benchmarks will look like the old ~400 ms again (expected).

Run a **third** benchmark pass: Tier 1 on + Tier 2 on. That’s what you’d ship if both help, and it avoids guessing which layer earned the win.

**One nuance**

Tier 2 can still use a **background thread** without Tier 1’s session cache — those aren’t the same feature. Your numbers match what the code is actually doing. Tier 2 didn’t fail — it just doesn’t touch the slow parts you’re feeling.

## What Tier 2 actually does

**One change only:** when search looks for nodes whose label matches a keyword, it uses a sorted word index instead of looping over every node’s label in memory.

```
Search today (Tier 2 on, Tier 1 off):

1. Fetch ALL ~10,026 nodes from SQLite     ← still every search (~350–400 ms)
2. Build/rebuild token index in RAM       ← extra work on first search after import/edit
3. findNodesByLabel via index             ← was already fast; saves maybe a few ms
4. Graph expansion + ranking               ← unchanged
```

Your benchmarks (~383–397 ms search vs ~414 ms baseline) say step 3 was never the bottleneck. Almost all the time is still step 1.

Tier 2 was meant to fix: *“don’t scan all 10k labels to find keyword matches.”*  
At 10k nodes that in-memory scan was already cheap. The expensive part is loading 10k SwiftData objects from disk every time.

## What Tier 2 does **not** touch

| What you noticed | Handled by Tier 2? | What actually fixed it before |
|------------------|-------------------|-------------------------------|
| Search ~400 ms | Barely | **Tier 1** — cache nodes in RAM, search off main thread |
| All Contacts 4–5 s open | **No** | **Tier 1** — cache master list, skip refetch when graph unchanged |
| Back from node → All Contacts delay | **No** | **Tier 1** — skip reload when browse fingerprint unchanged |
| Favorite + back delay | **No** | **Tier 1** — browse cache ignores edit-only changes |

With Tier 1 off, browse screens are back to: fetch all nodes → filter masters → sort → build the list. That’s the 4–5 second delay, with or without Tier 2.

## How to read your numbers

| Test | Pre–Tier 1 | Tier 2 alone | Tier 1 alone (earlier) |
|------|------------|--------------|------------------------|
| Search all | ~414 ms | ~385–397 ms | ~48 ms |
| Search masters | ~405 ms | ~370–390 ms | ~50 ms |
| All Contacts | slow | slow (4–5 s) | instant |

Tier 2 alone ≈ baseline for search, and browse is slow because Tier 1 browse cache is off. That’s expected.

## Bottom line

- **Tier 1** = session cache + background search + browse list cache → big wins everywhere you measured.
- **Tier 2** = faster label lookup **after** you’ve already loaded the whole graph → small win in theory, not visible in practice.

Tier 2 only pays off if we **stop fetching all nodes** first (index tells us which IDs to load), or combine it with Tier 1’s cache so the index runs on data already in RAM and search stays off the main thread.

## Sensible next step

1. **Re-enable Tier 1** (`performanceTier1Enabled = true`, keep Tier 2 on).
2. Re-run benchmarks — that’s the realistic production combo.
3. Decide whether Tier 2 adds anything on top of Tier 1’s ~48 ms searches. If not, Tier 2 may not be worth shipping alone.

I can flip the flags and add a “Tier 2 alone” section to your notes with these numbers if you want.

## Tier 2, as we built it, does not improve anything you can feel

You’re not missing a test. With Tier 1 off, Tier 2 doesn’t make the app feel better in any normal use.

It only changes one internal step: *after* all ~10k nodes are already loaded from the database, it finds label matches a bit faster. That step was never what made search feel slow. Loading 10k nodes from SQLite is.

- **Search** — your ~385–400 ms vs ~414 ms baseline is basically noise. You won’t feel that.
- **All Contacts** — Tier 2 never touches this. Still slow without Tier 1.
- **Open a contact → back to All Contacts** — same. Tier 2 doesn’t help.
- **Favorite → back** — same.

There is no Test app workflow where Tier 2 alone should feel clearly better. Your experience matches the code.

## What Tier 1 improves (this is what users feel)

| What to try | No tiers | Tier 1 only |
|-------------|----------|-------------|
| Home search after stress import | ~½ second lag per search | Near-instant after first search |
| Menu → Benchmarks → Search all `"1021"` | ~400 ms | ~50 ms |
| All Contacts first open | Several seconds | Fast |

| Favorite someone → back to All Contacts | Slow refetch | Stays fast |

That’s what Tier 1 was for. You already measured it (~48 ms search, instant All Contacts).

## Does Tier 2 only help Tier 1?

**With the current implementation: practically yes — and even then, barely.**

Tier 1 keeps the graph in RAM so repeat searches skip the big database load. Tier 2 then speeds up label matching on that in-memory data. But label matching on 10k nodes in RAM was already fast once Tier 1 cached them. So Tier 1 + Tier 2 together would likely still feel like **Tier 1 alone** — maybe a few milliseconds in Benchmarks, not something you’d notice tapping around.

Tier 2 would only stand on its own if we redesigned it to **use the index to avoid loading all nodes** (load only candidates from the DB). We didn’t build that.

## What you actually need to test (practical)

**If deciding what to ship:**

1. **Tier 1 on, Tier 2 off** — run your normal Test app flow (search, All Contacts, back navigation). That’s the UX bar.
2. **Tier 1 on, Tier 2 on** — same flow. If you can’t tell the difference, Tier 2 isn’t earning its keep.
3. **Tier 2 alone** — not worth UX testing; benchmarks already showed it doesn’t move the needle.

**Honest recommendation:** Don’t add Tier 2 to production as it exists now. It’s extra code with no user-visible benefit. Ship **Tier 1** when you’re ready; drop or shelve Tier 2 unless you want to rebuild it so the index replaces the full-node fetch.

On the general notes on the masters, does changing the max characters from 500 to 1,000 add any wait to the app when they are empty?  E.g. memory does keep a placeholder that there MAY be 1,000 characters at some point slowing down the app?

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT

[REDACTED]

ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
[REDACTED]

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
No — raising the max from 500 to 1,000 does **not** slow the app or reserve memory when General Info is empty.

**How it’s stored**

`generalInfo` on each `Node` is an optional `String?` in SwiftData. When empty it’s usually `nil` or `""` — not a fixed 500- or 1,000-character block. SQLite stores only what’s actually there.

**What the 500 limit does today**

It’s only a **cap at edit/save time** in `InputLimits.generalInfo`:

- Truncates while typing in the General Info editor  
- Truncates again in `sanitizeGeneralInfo` when saving  

Nothing pre-allocates 500 characters per master. Changing that constant to 1,000 just allows longer text when someone actually types it.

**When it could matter (only with real data)**

- **Filled notes** — more characters per node means slightly more disk and RAM when those nodes are loaded (your 1k benchmark with 250-char notes on masters is an example of that).  
- **Empty notes** — essentially no difference between 500 max and 1,000 max.

General Info also isn’t used in search, so a higher limit doesn’t affect search performance.

**Bottom line:** Safe to bump to 1,000 for the next build. Empty fields stay lightweight; you only pay a bit more storage/memory for contacts that actually have long notes.

[REDACTED]

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT

**Mostly it’s just more characters — not a special “General Info engine” that’s slow.**

General Info is a normal optional string on each `Node` (`generalInfo: String?`), same idea as phone or email. There’s no separate notes table, index, or search pass. Empty = `nil` or `""`; filled = however many characters you actually saved.

### What “more weight” meant in the benchmarks

| Effect | Why |
|--------|-----|
| **Bigger JSON file** | 1,000 × 250 `x`s ≈ **250 KB** of note text alone (+ JSON quoting/overhead). That’s why the 1k file grew vs the 10k file (~5.2 MB vs ~4.1 MB). |
| **Slightly more import work** | Import reads/writes those strings into SQLite — more bytes to parse and store. Your import was still ~6 s either way. |
| **More RAM when loading nodes** | Any code that `fetch`es **all** `Node` rows loads `generalInfo` along with label, dates, etc., even when it doesn’t use notes. |

### What it does **not** do (today)

- **Not used in search** — `SearchService` never reads `generalInfo`.
- **Not in the performance snapshot** — Tier 1’s search cache doesn’t include notes in the snapshot.
- **Not scanned on Home / All Contacts** — only shown on the Master page (preview + editor).

So your ~449 ms search on the 1k benchmark wasn’t “notes search is slow.” It’s still “load ~11k nodes + graph search,” same class as the 10k test. Notes might add a **little** I/O/memory on that full fetch, but they’re not a separate structural bottleneck.

### Could anything be optimized?

Only in a **bulk-load** sense, not because General Info is designed badly:

- Today, search/browse often loads **whole** `Node` objects, so long notes ride along in memory even when unused.
- A future optimization could lazy-load notes or fetch lighter fields for list/search — that would help **large graphs with long notes**, not empty notes.

**Bottom line:** The benchmark impact was **character count + more nodes/connections in that file**, not a special General Info structure worth optimizing on its own. Raising the limit to 1,000 doesn’t reserve space or slow empty notes; it only matters when users actually type long notes, and even then search behavior doesn’t change.

Explain how lazy-load works for general notes, and explain what "lazy-load" means in general as I have seen you use that term before.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lazy-load** means: **don’t load something until something actually needs it.**

You load the minimum up front, and fetch the rest only when the user (or code) opens the part that needs it.

---

## Lazy-load in general

**Eager load (what you often do today):**  
When you open a contact list, the app loads **everything** on each record — name, dates, phone, email, **and** a 1,000-character note — even if you never tap that contact.

**Lazy load:**  
When you open the list, you load only what the list needs (e.g. display name, id). The note stays on disk until you tap that Master and open General Info — **then** you load the note.

Everyday analogy: a library catalog card vs the full book. The catalog gives you title and shelf number; you only pull the book off the shelf when someone asks to read it.

Developers use “lazy” for the same idea in other places:

- **Images on a long webpage** — thumbnails load as you scroll, not all 500 images at once.
- **App screens** — a menu item’s detail view isn’t built until you tap it.
- **Database fields** — load a short row for lists; load the big text field only on the detail screen.

Opposite terms: **eager load** (load everything early) or **prefetch** (load ahead on purpose because you expect to need it soon).

---

## How your app works today (not lazy for notes)

Each contact is one `Node` in SwiftData. `generalInfo` is a normal string field on that same object — like `label` or `phoneNumber`.

When code runs something like “fetch all nodes” for search or All Contacts, SwiftData typically loads **whole** `Node` records from SQLite. That includes `generalInfo` even though:

- Home search **doesn’t** search notes  
- All Contacts **doesn’t** show notes  
- Only the Master page shows/edits notes  

So if 1,000 masters each have 250–1,000 characters of notes, those characters are still **read into memory** whenever the app loads all nodes — even when notes aren’t used on that screen. That’s extra disk I/O and RAM, not a separate “notes subsystem,” just **bulk loading the full row**.

---

## How lazy-load *could* work for General Info (conceptually)

You’d split “list/search data” from “notes data.” For example:

1. **List / search** loads lightweight data: id, labels, connections, flags — **no** `generalInfo`.
2. User opens a Master → app loads **that one** node’s `generalInfo` (or only that field) for the preview/editor.
3. User goes back → note can stay cached for that contact or be dropped from memory; either way you didn’t load 1,000 notes during search.

Ways to do that in practice (high level):

- **Separate storage** — notes in another table/entity, linked by node id; fetch notes only when opening the editor.
- **Fetch only certain fields** — if the stack supports it, list queries omit the big column (not always easy with SwiftData’s model-as-one-object style).
- **On-demand fetch** — Master page: `fetch(nodeId)` when appearing; search: never touch `generalInfo`.

Nothing like that is implemented today. Notes are just another column on `Node`, loaded whenever the full node is loaded.

---

## What lazy-load would and wouldn’t fix

| Would help | Wouldn’t help |
|------------|----------------|
| Search / All Contacts when many contacts have **long** notes | Empty notes (nothing extra to load anyway) |
| Memory when scanning thousands of nodes | Import time (import still has to write every note to the database) |
| Backup JSON size on disk | — (file size is still the actual text you stored) |

---

## Short summary

- **Lazy-load** = load later, only when needed.  
- **Your app today** = notes ride along whenever a full `Node` is fetched, even when that screen doesn’t use them.  
- **Lazy General Info** = load notes only when opening that Master’s General Info (or that contact’s detail), not during every “load all contacts” or search pass.

For normal personal use with short or empty notes, the difference is tiny. It matters more at expo scale with lots of long notes — which is closer to the Directories product than today’s main app.

## In-app vs App Store (two separate jobs)

| | **In-app** (wording in the app) | **App Store** (store page) |
|--|--------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **What** | Buttons, menu, How-To, paywall, settings, errors | Name, subtitle, description, keywords, What’s New, screenshots |
| **How you add it** | Translator returns `.strings` files → we add `es.lproj`, etc. in **Xcode** → rebuild | **App Store Connect** web UI — add each language, paste text **per language** |
| **One file loads both?** | **No** | **No** |
| **Automatic from app strings?** | **No** | **No** |

**App Store:** There’s no single upload that localizes the listing from the app. You (or a translator) provide text for each language; you paste it into App Store Connect for that locale. Some teams use Fastlane/metadata folders, but it’s still separate from in-app `.strings`.

**In-app:** Translator gets `Localizable.strings` (keys = English on the left, translations on the right). We drop each language into Xcode and ship a new build. Device language picks the right `.lproj`.

Yes — that’s the idea, with one nuance: App Store copy is **not** a `.strings` key file like the app. It’s a **short set of labeled fields** you copy out once, get translated, then paste back **per language in App Store Connect**.

### What you do for App Store marketing text

1. **Copy your current English listing** from App Store Connect (what’s live now):
   - App name (if localized)
   - Subtitle
   - Description
   - Keywords
   - Promotional text (if any)
   - What’s New (for the version you’re shipping — can wait until submit)

2. **Put that in one place for the translator** — not Xcode. For example:
   - `If I Must Localization/app-store-connect/en.md`  
   or a simple doc with sections like **Subtitle**, **Description**, **Keywords**.

   Translators don’t need “keys” like `"Add" = "..."`. They need **field labels + English text + translated text**.

3. **Translator returns** the same fields in Spanish, French, etc. (separate file per language, or one spreadsheet).

4. **You (or we) paste into App Store Connect** for each language:
   - App → **App Information** (and/or the version page) → **Localizations** → **+ Language** → fill each field → save.

That step is **always in App Store Connect**, not in Xcode. A new app build does **not** update the store description.

### So your mental model

| | In-app | App Store |
|--|--------|-----------|
| English master | `source/en/Localizable.strings` | Copy from ASC → `app-store-connect/en.md` |
| Translator deliverable | `Localizable.strings` per language | Same fields translated (doc or table) |
| Where it goes | Xcode `xx.lproj` | App Store Connect, **manual paste per language** |

### Do you *have* to make a “key set”?

**Practically yes** — you need **one English snapshot** of what’s in ASC now so translators aren’t guessing. It doesn’t have to be technical keys; labeled sections are enough.

You don’t have to duplicate work inside ASC until translations are ready: English stays as-is; you only **add** languages and paste translated text when you have it.

### Optional help from me

When you’re ready, you can paste your current App Store English (subtitle, description, keywords, etc.) here or into `app-store-connect/en.md`, and I can:

- Format it for translators  
- Add matching `es.md` / `fr.md` templates  
- Give you a checklist of exactly which ASC screens to paste into  

**In-app** and **App Store** can use the **same language list**, but they’re **two separate translation jobs** and **two separate places to apply them** (Xcode vs App Store Connect).

Based on Google’s message, there are two limits:

1. **5 requests per second** (burst) — this is almost certainly what you hit. With 12 parallel workers, the script was sending far more than 5/sec.
2. **200k requests per day** — you used roughly **8–9k** (~25 locales × ~332 strings), so the daily cap is not the issue.

**How long to wait:** **A few hours is usually enough**, not a full day. IP throttling from the free endpoint often clears in **2–6 hours**; waiting **overnight** is a safe buffer if you want zero risk of immediate re-throttling.

**When you resume (not now):**
- Pick up from `translations/.cache.json` — only the remaining ~24 locales need work.
- Go **slow**: ~3–4 requests/sec max (e.g. 1 worker, ~250–300 ms between calls), or use `translate_batch` in small chunks.
- Run **one locale at a time** with a short pause between locales.

No action needed right now; localization stays paused until you say to continue.

## 1. Guideline 3.1.2(c) — Missing Terms of Use in metadata

- Privacy: https://ifimust.com/privacy.html  
- Terms: https://ifimust.com/terms.html  

**Do this in App Store Connect:**

1. **App Information → Privacy Policy URL**  
   Set: `https://ifimust.com/privacy.html` (if not already).

2. **App Description (English + every localized description)**  
   Add at the **end** of the description (Apple wants it in the description text, not only in-app):

   ```
   Subscription required for full access. If I Must Premium is an auto-renewable annual subscription. A 2-week free trial is available for eligible new subscribers; then $4.99/year (price may vary by region). Payment is charged to your Apple ID. Subscription auto-renews unless canceled at least 24 hours before the end of the current period. Manage or cancel in Settings → Apple ID → Subscriptions.

   Privacy Policy: https://ifimust.com/privacy.html
   Terms of Use: https://ifimust.com/terms.html
   ```

3. **EULA field (optional)**  
   - If you use **Apple’s standard EULA**, you still need the Terms link **in the description** (above).

## 2. Guideline 2.3.2 — Paid features not clearly labeled in metadata

Screenshots that only show Home/Master/search with no paywall context are a common cause of 2.3.2 rejections.

Your read is close. It’s less “the app forgot which direction you came from” and more **navigation stack + stale Home search state** after deletes.

## What’s likely crashing

Two things overlap:

**1. Home search results are stale**

When you search `"t"`, Home keeps live `[Node]` objects in `searchResults`. That list is **not refreshed** when you:
- open a Master from search,
- delete contacts,
- or pop back to Home.

So after both deletes, Home can still show `"test test"` / `"tom test"` in the results box even though those rows are gone from the database. SwiftUI may then touch **deleted SwiftData objects** when Home redraws → crash.

**2. Delete pops one level, but the deleted node may still be “active” in the stack**

Delete does `router.path.removeLast()` after removing the node from SwiftData. If the screen you’re on is the node being deleted, NavigationStack can briefly still be tied to that `PersistentIdentifier` while Home underneath still holds old search rows. That’s a classic “delete the thing you’re viewing” timing issue.

Your two repro paths both end the same way:

| Path | What happens |
|------|----------------|
| A: delete `tom test` → auto back to `test test` → delete `test test` | Pop to Home with stale `"t"` results |
| B: delete `tom test` → back to `test test` → back Home → tap `test test` in search → delete | Same: delete + pop while search still holds old nodes |

Data is deleted correctly; the crash is almost certainly **UI state**, not failed deletion.

---

## Is keeping the last search open necessary?

**No — it’s a convenience choice, not a requirement.**

Right now it behaves like a “search session”: leave Home, come back, `"t"` and results are still there. That’s nice if you’re browsing several matches, but it’s risky when the graph changes underneath (delete, link changes, import, etc.).

---

## Would clearing search when tapping a result be better?

**Partly.** Clearing `searchText` + `searchResults` when you open a contact from search would avoid the “tap a ghost row after delete” path (your path B).

It would **not fully fix** path A by itself, because after the second delete you still land on Home with the old `"t"` list unless you also refresh or clear on delete.

---

## Would a clean Home after delete be better?

**Yes — that’s the strongest fix conceptually.**

After a successful delete, something like:
- pop to Home cleanly (`path = NavigationPath()` or ensure empty stack), and
- **either** clear search, **or** re-run the current query and drop missing nodes

…would match user expectation (“that contact is gone”) and avoid stale `Node` references.

A small extra guard: when building search results / connection links, skip IDs that no longer exist in the model context.

---

## Recommendation (when you’re ready to fix)

| Priority | Change | Why |
|----------|--------|-----|
| 1 | On delete success: go to clean Home + clear or refresh search | Fixes both repro paths |
| 2 | Filter search results against live model (or store IDs and resolve on tap) | Prevents ghost rows |
| 3 | Optional: clear search when opening a Master from search | Nice UX; reduces stale state |

I would **not** only tweak back-button behavior; the root issue is **search results outliving deleted nodes**.

---

## UX opinion

- **Keep search after back:** OK for power users, but needs refresh on graph changes.
- **Clear on navigate to Master:** simpler mental model (“search was a launcher”).
- **Clear/refresh after delete:** best alignment with “this person is gone.”

When you want to implement, the smallest high-impact change is probably in `deleteCurrentNodeAndPop()`: after save, reset navigation to Home and invalidate/refresh search — not just `removeLast()`.

## Languages in Xcode vs ASC — your question

**Yes — you can keep all `.lproj` files in Xcode without translating ASC copy.**

They are separate systems:

| | In Xcode (`.lproj`) | App Store Connect |
|--|---------------------|-------------------|
| **What it affects** | In-app UI (buttons, paywall, How-To, etc.) | Store listing (description, subtitle, keywords, screenshots per locale) |
| **Required together?** | No | No |
| **If you ship `.lproj` but only English ASC** | French device → French in-app UI | French App Store page can still show **English** listing text until you paste translations |

When you upload a build, ASC **detects** which languages are in the binary. You do **not** have to fill every language’s description before submit. English metadata + rejection fixes is enough for resubmission.

**Practical approach for this build:**
- **Keep** `.lproj` in the project (already done; no harm).
- **Only update English ASC** for the rejection (subscription disclosure, Terms/Privacy links, promotional text, paywall screenshot).
- **Defer** pasting `ASC-Copy-All-Languages.txt` into other locales until you have time.

If you want to **minimize scope**, you could remove extra `.lproj` folders before submit — but that’s extra work and you lose in-app localization for those languages. Keeping them loaded is fine.

**Short answer: No — the search/delete fix does not touch Tier 1 code, and nothing in Tier 1 needs to change because of it.**

---

### Why

The fix only changed:

- **`AppRouter`** — `resetToHomeAfterDelete()` (navigation + signal to clear search)
- **`ContentView`** — `clearHomeSearch()` on result tap and after delete
- **`NodeDetailView`** — delete calls `resetToHomeAfterDelete()` instead of `removeLast()`

Tier 1 lives in `GraphPerformanceCache` / `GraphPerformanceTier1` and is used only when `AppBuildConfig.usesPerformanceTier1` is **on**. That flag is still **off**, so Production (and normal Test use) still goes through `SearchService.rankedSearch` — same as before, plus the new clear/reset behavior.

Clearing `searchResults` and canceling the debounce task is UI state only; it doesn’t bypass or alter the Tier 1 search path.

---

### When you turn Tier 1 on later

One **existing** gap (not caused by this fix): single-contact delete does **not** call `AppBuildConfig.invalidatePerformanceCaches()`. Bulk delete/import in `GraphImportExport` does.

So when you enable Tier 1 for Production, it’s worth adding cache invalidation after a successful Master delete (and optionally after add/edit). That keeps the session snapshot in sync with the graph. Your new “clear search on delete” already avoids showing stale rows on Home; cache invalidation would keep **background search** correct if someone searches again without leaving Home.

**Suggested one-liner when Tier 1 ships** (in `deleteCurrentNodeAndPop`, after `save()`):

```swift
AppBuildConfig.invalidatePerformanceCaches()
```


Ok, that made the copy function pop up and when copied it did copy the who master name and past, but the blue highlighter that people are used to did not pop up with the two ends that allows you to highlight all or part.  Why is that?  I don't really need it fixed, I was just curious.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
What you’re seeing is normal for **read-only SwiftUI `Text`**, not a bug in your app.

### Two different selection systems

| | **Master title (`Text` + `.textSelection(.enabled)`)** | **Pencil mode (`TextField`)** |
|--|--|--|
| **Underlying control** | Static label with selection enabled | Real text field (editing) |
| **Typical UX** | Long-press → **Copy** / **Select All** menu; may copy the whole line | Blue highlight + **draggable handles** for partial selection |
| **Purpose** | “Let people copy this label” | “Let people edit this text” |

The pencil path uses **UITextField**-style editing, which is the full iOS text UI people know (carets, blue selection, drag the ends).

The title path uses **selection on static `Text`**. Apple treats that as “copy this content,” not “edit this document,” so on iPhone it often **skips the full handle UI** and goes straight to a context menu or selects the whole string when you copy.

### Why you still got a correct copy

`.textSelection(.enabled)` turned on *some* selection behavior — enough for **Copy** and the full display name (“tom tall”) — without exposing the fine-grained highlight/handle chrome that editable fields get.

### If you ever wanted the full handle UI on the title

You’d need something editable or text-view–like (e.g. keep using the pencil `TextField`, or a read-only `UITextView` / `TextEditor` hack). For a contact title, the menu-style copy is usually what Apple intends for static labels.

So: **copy works; the missing blue bars are because it’s display text, not an editor.** No fix needed for your use case.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is almost certainly **not Apple wiping your memory** — it’s **your production paywall/subscription check tearing down and rebuilding the whole app UI**.

## Why it happens (1.0 Production)

In `RootView`, when you’re **not** on the Test app, the screen switches on subscription state:

```27:36:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
                    switch subscriptionManager.accessState {
                    case .loading:
                        ProgressView(L10n.tr("Loading…"))
                    case .needsSubscription:
                        PaywallView()
                    case .subscribed:
                        ContentView()
                    }
```

Every time the app becomes active again (leave app → return, or sometimes on launch), this runs:

```41:44:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, newPhase in
            guard newPhase == .active else { return }
            Task { await subscriptionManager.refresh() }
```

And `refresh()` **always** does this first:

```38:42:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/SubscriptionManager.swift
    func refresh() async {
        accessState = .loading
        ...
        accessState = hasAccess ? .subscribed : .needsSubscription
```

So on resume:

1. `accessState` → **loading** → `ContentView` is **removed** (replaced by spinner)
2. `NavigationStack` + `router.path` (Master, lists, etc.) are **destroyed**
3. StoreKit finishes → **subscribed** → **new** `ContentView` → fresh Home

That looks like a quick **flash/reload back to Home**. Same idea on first open: loading → subscribed flash.

## Why Test app doesn’t do it

Test **always** skips the paywall and shows `ContentView` directly — no subscription switch, no remount on resume.

## Why “beta production” might not have shown it

If that was **If I Must Test**, or TestFlight but you didn’t background the app much, or the spinner was so brief you didn’t notice — same code can feel fine in testing and bad in daily use.

## Delete → Home flash

- **1.0:** Delete uses `removeLast()` (pop one level). A **flash to Home** on delete can still happen if `refresh()` runs around the same time and remounts `ContentView`.
- **1.1 (pending):** Delete **intentionally** resets to Home (`resetToHomeAfterDelete`) — that part is by design; the **resume** issue is separate.

## Should you wait for 1.1?

**1.1 does not fix the resume-to-Home flash** — same `refresh()` → `.loading` logic is still there.

So:

| Issue | Fixed in 1.1? |
|--------|----------------|
| Resume from Master → flash to Home | **No** (likely still there) |
| Delete → clean Home + clear search | **Yes** (intentional) |
| Launch flash | **Maybe slightly**; same root cause may remain |

Worth **spot-checking 1.1 on a real device** once it’s on TestFlight/App Store: open a Master → Home button → background app → return. If it still jumps to Home, we should patch.

## Proper fix (for a small 1.1.1 or next build)

Don’t set `accessState = .loading` on **foreground refresh** if the user is already subscribed — re-check entitlements **in the background** and only change state if access actually changed. Keep `ContentView` mounted so navigation survives.

That’s standard for subscription apps — not special “memory hold” from Apple; just **don’t destroy the navigation stack while validating the subscription**.

---

**Bottom line:** Not required Apple behavior; it’s the subscription refresh UX. Waiting for 1.1 is fine for the **delete/search** fixes, but **don’t assume 1.1 fixes backgrounding on a Master**. If you want, after 1.1 ships we can apply the silent refresh fix in a quick follow-up build.

## One underlying bug (cases 2–4, and part of case 1)

```41:44:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, newPhase in
            guard newPhase == .active else { return }

        }
```

`refresh()` immediately sets `accessState = .loading`, which **replaces** `ContentView` with a loading spinner:

```38:42:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/SubscriptionManager.swift
    func refresh() async {
        accessState = .loading
        await loadProduct()
        let hasAccess = await hasActiveSubscription()
        accessState = hasAccess ? .subscribed : .needsSubscription
```

`ContentView` owns the `NavigationStack` and `AppRouter`, so that remount wipes navigation and you land on Home — often with a visible flash. **If I Must Test** does not hit this because the paywall is bypassed and `ContentView` never gets torn down.

Your instinct is right — there is a real gap between what the **code accepts** and what several **translations tell users**, especially in Japanese and Chinese.

Full audit report saved at: `If I Must Localization/L10n-Punctuation-Audit.txt`

---

## What the app actually accepts today

Add Contact / Add Info fields only allow **ASCII** punctuation for the two operators:

```38:41:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/InputSanitization.swift
    private static func isAllowedAddEditCharacter(_ char: Character) -> Bool {
        if char == " " || char == "." || char == "," || char == "/" || char == "-" { return true }
        if char.isLetter || char.isNumber { return true }
        return false
```

The parser only splits on ASCII comma and treats ASCII period as the concatenate operator:

```39:39:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/AddInputParser.swift
        let rawGroups = trimmed.split(separator: ",").map { String($0).trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces) }
```

```62:62:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/AddInputParser.swift
            if ch == "." {
```

**Blocked characters are stripped silently** while typing — no error, they just disappear.

Submit-time sanitization does run NFKC normalization, but that never helps here because non-ASCII punctuation is removed **before** submit.

### Characters users might naturally type (not accepted today)

| Character | Name | Typical use |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `，` U+FF0C | Full-width comma | Chinese/Japanese keyboard |
| `．` U+FF0E | Full-width period | Chinese/Japanese keyboard |
| `。` U+3002 | Ideographic full stop | Japanese/Chinese sentence period |
| `、` U+3001 | Enumeration comma | Japanese list separator |

If a Japanese user types `東京。大阪` intending `tokyo.osaka`, the `。` is stripped and they get `東京大阪` — concatenate silently fails.

---

## What the translations say

### Japanese / Chinese — mismatch with code

Several How-To strings tell users to use **ideographic period `。`**, not ASCII `.`:

| English source | Japanese translation (problem) |
|----------------|------------------------------|
| "Use . to concatenate words" | `使用 。単語を連結する` |
| "Concatenate: use . between words" | `連結: を使用します。単語の間` (the `.` got absorbed into Japanese sentence punctuation) |

Same pattern in **zh-Hans** and **zh-Hant** (`使用 。连接单词`).

So users in those locales are being **instructed to use a character the app rejects**.

### Korean, Thai, Vietnamese — mostly OK

Instructions still show ASCII `.` in examples (`new.york`, `使用 .`). Examples use ASCII `,` in input samples like `,john tall`.

### Japanese / Chinese comma examples — mixed

Prose uses native punctuation (`、` or `，`) in examples like `john Tall、Sally short`, but the **actual input examples** that matter still use ASCII `,` in `,john tall` — good for function, confusing in prose.

### Allowed-characters strings

Translations describe "句号/句点/ピリオド" (period) and "逗号/カンマ" (comma) in **generic** terms — they do not say "ASCII only" or mention full-width equivalents.

---

## Severity assessment

| Issue | Impact |
|-------|--------|
| User types `。` or `，` per How-To | Concatenate / multi-contact **silently fails** — frustrating, no error |
| User types full-width on CJK keyboard | Same — characters stripped |
| Translation tells user wrong symbol | **ja / zh-Hans / zh-Hant** — documentation bug on top of code gap |
| Western locales | Low risk — keyboards default to ASCII `.` and `,` |

This is **not** an App Review localization rejection issue. It is a **UX / correctness** issue for CJK users.

---

## Recommended fix (ship with Refresh Fix + l10n build)

**1. Code — silent normalize (preferred, no How-To change required)**

In `normalizeAddEditTyping` (before the allowlist filter), map:

- `．` → `.` (full-width period)
- `，` → `,` (full-width comma)
- `。` → `.` (ideographic full stop — treat as concatenate operator in this context)
- `、` → `,` (enumeration comma — treat as group separator)

Then run the existing ASCII allowlist and parser unchanged. Users get natural keyboard behavior without reading a footnote.

**2. Translations — fix ja/zh How-To strings**

Re-translate the ~7 ja + ~5 zh keys so instructions explicitly show **`.`** (or say "period (`.` or `。`)" if you want both visible). Right now Google mangled `use .` into Japanese sentence structure.

**3. How-To — optional, not required if (1) ships**

If you normalize silently, you do **not** need a How-To disclaimer. If you want belt-and-suspenders for CJK locales only, one line in English master:

> "Full-width period and comma (。．，) work the same as . and ,."

Then retranslate that key for ja/zh/ko.

I'd skip calling it out in Western locales — unnecessary noise.

---

## What I would **not** do

- Don't broaden the allowlist to all Unicode punctuation — keep the narrow operator set.
- Don't change the parser to split on `、` for Japanese only — normalize to `,` instead; one code path.
- Don't block on this for 1.1 review — bundle with the next binary alongside Refresh Fix.

---

## Summary

Your concern is valid. The app is **English-punctuation-only** at input time, while **ja/zh translations often point users at `。`** and CJK keyboards naturally produce full-width forms. The fix is small: normalize those four characters before filtering, then clean up the misleading How-To strings in ja/zh.

Want me to queue this as a P1.5 item in `If-I-Must-App-NOTES.md` for the same submission as Refresh Fix, or implement when you give the go-ahead after review?

## 1. Did I review all languages?

**Now:** A **full audit of all 49 non-English locales** is done. Report: `If I Must Localization/L10n-Punctuation-Audit-All-Locales.txt`

| Region | Issue |
|--------|--------|
| **ja, zh-Hans, zh-Hant** | Worst — How-To often said `使用 。` instead of `.`; users were steered toward characters the app rejected |
| **hi, bn, ur** | Devanagari/Arabic danda/comma in instructions (`।`) — matched natural typing but was blocked in code |
| **ko, th, vi, id, ms** | Mostly OK in examples; some awkward machine phrasing |
| **European (de, fr, es, it, pl, …)** | Generally fine — ASCII `.` and `,` are natural on those keyboards |
| **he, ar** | Arabic comma `،` in prose; input examples still used ASCII `,` |
| **en-AU/CA/GB** | English variants — no punctuation issue |

**Root cause everywhere:** Code only accepted ASCII `.` and `,`, while several translations (especially CJK and Indic) pointed users at native marks.

---

## 2 & 3. Implemented now — allow native punctuation + explicit How-To

### Code (`InputSanitization.swift`)
Before filtering, these map silently to ASCII operators:

| Typed | Becomes |
|-------|---------|
| `．` `。` `।` `॥` | `.` (concatenate) |
| `，` `、` `，` `､` | `,` (group separator) |

- Native marks are **accepted**, not stripped
- **No blocked-character warning** for these (only truly invalid chars like `@` still warn)

All four warnings are addressed. Clean build shows no Swift warnings from your app code.

## What they were

### 1–2. `GraphPerformanceCache.swift` (Swift 6 actor isolation)

Your project uses `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor`, so everything defaults to the main actor. Tier 1 search runs work on a background thread via `Task.detached`, but `SearchSnapshotEngine.rankedSearchIDs` (and the linkable variant) were still treated as main-actor-only — a Swift 6 error.

**Fix:** Marked the snapshot search pipeline as explicitly `nonisolated` — `SearchSnapshotEngine`, the search sanitization path in `InputSanitization`, `SearchService.searchKeywords`, and `SearchTokenIndex.candidateNodeIDs`. Background search stays off the main thread; behavior unchanged.

### 3–4. `ReorderGrip.swift` (`UIScreen.main` deprecated in iOS 26)

Drag-row snapshots used `UIScreen.main.scale` for `ImageRenderer` and the floating drag image.

**Fix:** Switched to `@Environment(\.displayScale)`, which is the SwiftUI trait equivalent and works from view context.

Here’s a plain-language breakdown and how to label it for submission.

## What was going on

All four were **Xcode build warnings**, not bugs users reported. They showed up because the project targets newer Swift/iOS behavior (Swift 6 strict concurrency + iOS 26 APIs).

### Warnings 1 & 2 — `GraphPerformanceCache.swift`

**What:** Tier 1 search runs heavy work on a **background thread** (`Task.detached`) so the UI stays smooth. The search helper (`SearchSnapshotEngine`) was still treated as **main-thread-only** because the project defaults everything to the main actor.

**Risk if unfixed:** Fine today as warnings; in stricter Swift 6 mode it becomes a **compile error**. Could also cause subtle threading issues later.

**Fix:** Marked the snapshot search code as explicitly **safe to run off the main thread** (`nonisolated`) — same behavior, correct threading story.

### Warnings 3 & 4 — `ReorderGrip.swift`

**What:** Drag-to-reorder uses a snapshot of the row while you drag. It read screen scale from **`UIScreen.main`**, which Apple **deprecated in iOS 26**.

**Risk if unfixed:** Warning now; may break or behave wrong on future iOS versions.

**Fix:** Use SwiftUI’s **`displayScale`** from the view environment instead — the supported way to get pixel density in iOS 26+.

---

## What to call it when you submit

These are **not user-facing features**. Apple doesn’t need a special callout unless you’re filling internal release notes.

| Where | What to write |
|--------|----------------|
| **What’s New (App Store)** | Don’t mention — users won’t see a difference |
| **App Review notes** | Only if asked about warnings/build: *“Resolved Swift 6 concurrency warnings and iOS 26 API deprecations; no user-facing behavior change.”* |
| **Your own / internal label** | **“Swift 6 concurrency + iOS 26 deprecation cleanup”** or **“Build compatibility fixes”** |

If you bundle this with the next binary alongside **Refresh Fix** and **localization**, the public **What’s New** might look like:

> • Improved navigation when returning to the app  
> • Improved translations for several languages  
> • Stability and compatibility improvements  

The warning fixes fit under **“Stability and compatibility improvements”** — no need to name Swift concurrency or `UIScreen.main` for customers.

Short answer: **Xcode doesn’t keep a searchable warning history by date.** The Issues panel is mostly “right now,” not “what did I see on 6/11?”

## Why you only see 6/14 onward

The **Issues navigator** (and much of “Recent Issues”) reflects the **current project state** and **recent builds** in the active DerivedData folder. It is **not** an archive of every warning from every submission.

Build logs live here:

`~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/If_I_Must-…/Logs/Build/*.xcactivitylog`

Those get **rotated and replaced**. On your machine, the oldest retained logs in that folder are from **June 19** — nothing from the **6/11** archive build is still there unless you have a backup.

Your **6/11 archive** still exists:

`~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives/2026-06-11/If I Must 6-11-26, 3.15 AM.xcarchive`

But archives contain the **app binary + dSYMs**, not the compile warning list. Opening Organizer won’t show “warnings from that archive.”

---

## Ways you *might* recover old warnings

| Approach | Likelihood |
|----------|------------|
| **Report navigator (⌘9)** → pick an old build | Only if that build’s log still exists in DerivedData — unlikely for 6/11 |
| **Time Machine** backup of `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/` | Possible if you back up that folder |
| **Rebuild the old code** (git commit/tag from ~6/11) and build again | Best practical option — shows what *that code* would warn about *today* with current Xcode |
| **App Store Connect / TestFlight** | No compile warnings — Apple doesn’t store those |

There’s no Xcode setting like “show issues as of June 11, 2026.”

---

## Important: those 4 warnings did **not** cause the flash

Even if you found the 6/11 warning list, the four we fixed recently were:

1–2. **Swift 6 main-actor / background search** (`GraphPerformanceCache`)  
3–4. **`UIScreen.main` deprecated** (`ReorderGrip` drag snapshot)

Those are **compile-time / future-iOS compatibility** items. They don’t tear down navigation or send you Home.

The flash is explained by **runtime behavior** we already traced:

```41:44:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, newPhase in
            guard newPhase == .active else { return }
            Task { await subscriptionManager.refresh() }
        }
```

`refresh()` sets `accessState = .loading` → `ContentView` unmounts → navigation stack is destroyed → Home flash. That logic was in the 1.0 / 1.1 Production builds regardless of those four warnings.

**If I Must Test** skips the paywall path, so it often **doesn’t reproduce** the flash — which matches what you’ve seen.

---

## What actually fixes the flash

The **Refresh Fix (P1)** — silent subscription refresh when already subscribed, don’t set `.loading` on every resume. That’s separate from the warning cleanup and still pending until you give the go-ahead after review.

---

## If you still want to “see 6/11 warnings”

1. Check out the git commit you archived on **6/11** (if you have one).  
2. **Product → Clean Build Folder**, then **Build**.  
3. Read **Issues** or **Report navigator (⌘9)** for that build.

That tells you what **today’s Xcode** reports for **that old code** — close enough for peace of mind, but it won’t match the exact 6/11 log byte-for-byte.

## Why Test didn’t show the flash

**If I Must Test** always skips the paywall:

```24:26:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
                if PaywallGate.bypassesPaywall {

                } else {
```

`ContentView` (and your `NavigationStack`) **stay mounted the whole time**. Nothing tears them down on resume.

**Production If I Must** does this on every return to the app:

```41:44:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/RootView.swift
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, newPhase in
            guard newPhase == .active else { return }
            Task { await subscriptionManager.refresh() }
        }
```

And `refresh()` always does:

```38:42:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/SubscriptionManager.swift
    func refresh() async {
        accessState = .loading
        await loadProduct()
        let hasAccess = await hasActiveSubscription()
        accessState = hasAccess ? .subscribed : .needsSubscription
```

While `accessState == .loading`, Production shows a spinner **instead of** `ContentView` — navigation is destroyed. When refresh finishes, a **new** `ContentView` mounts at Home. That’s the flash.

So: **Test can’t reproduce this** unless you run the **If I Must** scheme with an active subscription. That’s expected, not a sign the diagnosis is wrong.

What you’re seeing — button spins briefly, then you’re back on the paywall — matches the code path pretty closely. It’s frustrating, but it doesn’t mean the flash diagnosis is wrong.

## What “spin, then refresh” probably is

When you tap **Start 2-Week Free Trial**:

1. Button shows spinner (`isPurchasing = true`)
2. StoreKit runs the purchase
3. App calls `refresh()` which sets **`accessState = .loading`** (full-screen “Loading…”)
4. App checks `Transaction.currentEntitlements`
5. If **no active entitlement** → back to paywall

So it can look like “nothing happened” when the purchase **didn’t stick in sandbox**, not when the app ignored you. Errors are sometimes silent too (`userCancelled`, or errors containing “cancel”).

---

## Why simulator sandbox often fails

Common causes:

| Issue | What to check |
|--------|----------------|
| **Wrong account type** | Sandbox login goes in **Settings → App Store → Sandbox Account** — not as the main Apple ID for the simulator |
| **Real Apple ID still signed in** | **Settings → App Store** — sign out of your real Apple ID on the simulator first |
| **New sandbox tester** | Create in App Store Connect → **Users and Access → Sandbox → Testers** (any email, doesn’t need to be real) |
| **Simulator flakiness** | Sandbox IAP on simulator is unreliable; **physical device** works more often |
| **No local StoreKit config** | Your project has **no `.storekit` file** — simulator depends entirely on Apple’s sandbox servers |

If the paywall shows **“If I Must Premium — $4.99/year…”** (not “Subscription is not available”), the product **is** loading — the failure is usually at **purchase / entitlement**, not product fetch.

---

## How to see what actually failed

1. Turn **Debug executable** back on (Scheme → Run → check “Debug executable”)
2. Run **If I Must** on simulator
3. Open **Xcode → Debug area → Console**
4. Filter for `Subscription`
5. Tap trial again

Look for lines like:
- `Purchase failed: …`
- `No product returned for …` (product problem)
- Or nothing after purchase → entitlement never appeared (typical sandbox issue)

**Not an Apple update** — this is a bug in our **Tier 1 performance** work, which shipped enabled in Production in build 37.

### What was happening

When you add a contact, it saves to the database correctly. Search, though, uses a **cached snapshot** of all nodes for speed. After an add, the cache noticed the graph had changed (node count went up) but then **rebuilt the snapshot from old in-memory nodes** instead of refetching from SwiftData. So search kept using stale data until a restart cleared the cache.

That matches your symptom exactly: add → search finds nothing → quit/reopen → search works.

### The fix

I updated `GraphPerformanceCache.ensureSearchCache` so it only uses the fast “edit-only” path when **node and connection counts are unchanged**. When structure changes (add/delete), it refetches from the database.

### How to verify

1. Add a contact on Home (e.g. `testname tall banker`)
2. Search `testname` immediately — should appear without restarting

This is ready for your **1.2** build alongside the notes editor tweaks. Want me to bump the build number?

Three separate issues — here’s what I found and what I changed.

---

### 1. Numbers in notes — fixed

This was a **Unicode/SDK change**, not something you did wrong. Recent Unicode data marks ASCII digits `0`–`9` as emoji. The notes filter (`General Info`, Home Drafts/Notes) blocks emoji — so digits were silently stripped.

Add Contact was unaffected because it explicitly allows `char.isNumber`.

**Fix:** ASCII digits are no longer treated as emoji in `InputSanitization`. Ready for your 1.2 build.

---

### 2. Allowing all characters in contacts/attributes — my opinion

**Security:** No real concern. Data stays on-device / iCloud; there’s no server to inject into.

**Practical risks** (not security):

| Risk | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|
| **Parser semantics** | Commas split masters, spaces split attributes, periods concatenate words (`new.york`). Extra punctuation can create unexpected graph structure. |
| **Search behavior** | Special characters become part of labels; search is word-prefix based, so odd symbols usually just don’t match. |
| **Lowercase storage** | Everything still normalizes to lowercase — `O'Brien` becomes `o'brien`. |
| **Export/import** | JSON backup handles Unicode; very exotic characters are fine but harder to read in a text file. |

**Recommendation:** Don’t open to literally *all* characters. A modest expansion is reasonable — e.g. `'` `&` `()` for names, `@` if people put emails in attributes. Keep blocking control characters and emoji in graph labels if you want consistency with notes. The meaningful constraint is **parser syntax**, not security.

If you want to go broader later, we could add a “free text” mode or escape rules — but that’s a product decision, not a safety one.

---

### 3. Offline use — partially fixed

Your contacts and Drafts/Notes are **already local** (SwiftData + UserDefaults). CloudKit syncs when online; it doesn’t require network to read/write locally.

What blocked you was the **subscription gate**: on launch, the app waited for StoreKit’s **product fetch** (needs network) before checking whether you’re subscribed. No cell service → stuck on “Loading…” → never reached Home or Drafts/Notes.

**Fix (in code for 1.2):**
- Remember last verified subscription state
- On launch, open the app immediately if previously subscribed
- Check entitlements **before** the network product fetch
- Load product pricing in the background when already subscribed

**Apple Notes comparison:** Once the app opens, behavior is similar — local first, sync later. The remaining gap: a **brand-new install** with no prior subscription still needs network once to subscribe. Existing subscribers should now get Home + Drafts/Notes offline.

**How to verify:** Subscribe once while online → enable airplane mode → force-quit → reopen → Home and Drafts/Notes should load.

---

All three fixes are in code for the **1.2** build (search cache fix from earlier + notes digits + offline launch). Want me to bump the build number?

**Recommendation: allow everything except control characters (including picture emojis).** That is the simpler, less convoluted path — and it avoids the Unicode trap that bit you with numbers.

---

### Why “no picture emojis, but all punctuation” is the *hard* path

The numbers bug wasn’t random. Unicode now marks many **ordinary text symbols** as emoji, not just 😀:

| Character | Blocked as “emoji” today? |
|-----------|---------------------------|
| `0`–`9` | Yes (we fixed with an ASCII-digit exemption) |
| `#` | **Yes** |
| `*` | **Yes** |
| `©` | **Yes** |
| `@`, `!`, `?`, `-`, `(`, `)` | No |
| `😀`, `👍` | Yes |

So “block emojis but allow all normal punctuation” means maintaining a growing **exemption list** — the opposite of avoiding per-language character research. You’d be playing whack-a-mole with every Unicode update.

**Allowing all emojis** (really: allow all printable text, strip only control chars) is *less* code than trying to filter picture emojis while keeping `#`, `*`, `©`, etc.

---

### Simplest code shape (if you proceed)

One shared rule everywhere (Add Contact, Add Info, General Info, Drafts/Notes):

> Strip control characters + enforce length limits. No allowlist. No emoji filter. No blocked-character warning.

That means you can **delete**:
- `isAllowedAddEditCharacter` / `filterAddEditLive` allowlist
- `isEmojiCharacter` entirely
- `AddEditInputFilterModifier` warning UI
- 2 localization keys × 49 languages (“Only letters…” + “Allowed characters…” in How-To)
- Most punctuation-normalization code *could* stay optional (maps `。` → `.` for parser convenience) — but it’s not required for “allow all”

**Revert later:** add a single flag in `AppBuildConfig` (e.g. `restrictAddEditCharacters`) defaulting to `false`. Flip to `true` to restore today’s allowlist + warnings. Or revert the commit. I’d document the flag in NOTES so you don’t have to remember the old behavior.

---

### Add/Edit vs Notes — two different systems today

| Area | Current rule | “Allow all” change |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| **Add Contact / Add Info** | Strict allowlist (letters, numbers, space, `.` `,` `/` `-`) + live strip + warning | Control chars only |
| **General Info / Drafts/Notes** | Block emoji + control chars | Control chars only (emoji filter goes away) |

Notes were already close to “allow all”; Add/Edit is where most code and UI complexity lives.

---

### Things that don’t change (worth knowing before you try it)

**Not a security issue** — still local data.

**Parser semantics still apply** even with all characters allowed:
- **Comma** = separate masters (`jack dad, jill mom`)
- **Space** = separate attributes
- **Period** = concatenate words (`new.york` → `new york`)

So `O'Brien` works fine, but a comma *inside* a name will still split groups. That’s graph syntax, not character filtering. Users may need a How-To line about commas/periods if we remove the “allowed characters” section.

**Search** still lowercases on save — emojis and symbols store as typed (after NFKC). Search may behave oddly on emoji-heavy labels, but nothing breaks.

---

### Full allowance vs expanded allowlist

| | Full allowance | Expanded allowlist (`@'&()` etc.) |
|--|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| Code | **Least** — one filter function | More — maintain a list |
| i18n | Remove limitation strings | Update limitation strings |
| Other languages | **No research needed** | Still chasing edge cases |
| Emoji | Allowed (including 😀) | Could allow or block — blocking reintroduces complexity |
| Risk | Messy contact names, parser surprises from `,` and `.` | Same parser risks, plus list never complete |

---

### Direct answer to your questions

1. **Prefer no picture emojis?** Understandable product preference, but **technically expensive** and fragile. `#` and `*` would be casualties unless we keep adding exemptions.

2. **Same issue as numbers for other characters?** Digits in **notes** yes (emoji filter). In **Add/Edit**, `@` and similar were blocked by the allowlist, not the emoji bug. Full allowance fixes both in one shot.

3. **Is allowing all emojis simpler if we allow all punctuation?** **Yes.** One rule beats two half-rules.

4. **Helps with other languages?** **Yes.** CJK punctuation, Arabic comma, Devanagari danda, etc. all just work — no normalization tables required (though keeping `。`→`.` normalization is still nice for the parser).

5. **Remove warnings + How-To + localizations?** **Yes**, if we go full allowance — those strings become wrong/misleading and should come out.

Question about O'brian before we Allow All, that is an apostrophy not a comma, so why would it split?

Checking how the parser treats apostrophes vs commas.

[REDACTED]

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ASSISTANT
------------------------------------------------------------------------
You're right — **O'Brien would not split.** I used a bad example.

The parser only treats three things specially:

| Character | Role |
|-----------|------|
| **Comma** `,` | Splits separate masters (`jack dad, jill mom` → two groups) |
| **Space** | Splits words within a group (`o'brien tall` → `o'brien` + `tall`) |
| **Period** `.` | Joins words (`new.york` → `new york`) |

An **apostrophe** `'` is just part of the word. `o'brien` stays one token and becomes one node label (stored lowercase as `o'brien`).

What *would* cause surprises with Allow All:

- A **comma inside a name** — e.g. `smith, jr tall` would split into two masters (`smith` and `jr tall`), not one name.
- A **period** between words — still triggers concatenation, not a literal period in the name (unless we change parser rules).

Apostrophes, hyphens, `@`, etc. are fine — they ride along inside a word. Sorry for the confusion on that earlier.

**Short answer:** You can’t turn off **Settings → Display & Text Size → Larger Text** for the whole phone. You *can* make **If I Must** ignore it and use only your in-app font control — and you’re **already partly doing that**.

### What your app does today

In `If_I_MustApp.swift`, the root view sets:

```29:29:/Users/randybevis/Desktop/If I Must/If I Must/If_I_MustApp.swift
                .environment(\.sizeCategory, AppFontSize.sizeCategory(for: fontSizeStep))
```

That tells SwiftUI: “use **Menu → App Settings → Text** (`fontSizeStep`), not the system Dynamic Type size.”

So for most of the app, **iPhone Settings font size should not apply** — only the in-app slider/steps should.

### Why your parents might still see huge text

1. **In-app Text setting** — They may have bumped it to **Large / iPad 1 / iPad 2** in your app (Menu → App Settings → Text).

2. **Your “Small” is still fairly big** — In `AppFontSize.swift`, even **X Small** maps to `.large`, and default **Small** maps to `.extraLarge`. So the app’s smallest size isn’t tiny.

3. **A few things can still follow the system** — Alerts, some sheets, keyboard, StoreKit paywall UI, and a few fixed toolbar fonts may not fully respect your override.

### How to lock it down further (if you want)

| Approach | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| Keep current `sizeCategory` override | Ignores system for most SwiftUI text |
| Add `.dynamicTypeSize(...)` at the root (iOS 15+) | Hard cap — e.g. only allow `.small` … `.xxLarge` from *your* steps |
| Map app steps from `.medium` instead of `.large` / `.extraLarge` | Makes “Small” actually smaller |
| Fixed point sizes everywhere | Full control, but worse accessibility and more work |

**Practical recommendation:** Check their **in-app** Text setting first (set to **X Small** or **Small**). If it’s still too big, we can tighten `AppFontSize` mapping and/or add a root `.dynamicTypeSize` cap so system Dynamic Type never bleeds through.

### Apple note

Apps are expected to respect accessibility, but offering **in-app font control** while ignoring system size is common and usually fine — especially since you already have Text settings in the app.

Want me to implement a stricter “ignore system Dynamic Type entirely” pass for 1.3?

**Sentence mode is in** — Master page, **Word** only.

### How it works
- Checkbox to the **right** of Add Info (unchecked by default)
- **Unchecked:** normal rules (spaces split words, `.` concatenates)

- Clears when you switch to Link or Make
- Hint under Show Hints explains it

**Yes — Call / Text / Email are wired correctly.** What you saw on Simulator is normal:

| Button | Opens | Simulator | Real iPhone |
|--------|--------|-----------|-------------|
| **Call** | Phone app (`tel:`) | Often does nothing — no cellular Phone app | Opens Phone with the number |

### 2. GitHub / getting this to Windows

**Why Cursor chats don’t show on Windows:** Agent chats stay on that machine’s Cursor account/workspace. They are **not** synced by opening the same folder on another PC. Specs/design/code only move if you copy them (or use Git).

| **Export this chat** (Cursor → export / copy transcript) into Specs if you want the discussion offline | Discussion text | Manual |
